title: Def Leppard Documentary 'Long Live Def Leppard' to Rock Theaters in 2027
summary:
They sold 110 million albums, packed stadiums, and survived tragedies that would have ended most bands. Now, Def Leppard's underdog story is heading to the big screen.

A new feature-length documentary called "Long Live Def Leppard" is slated for release in theaters in early 2027. It's the first-ever authorized film about the band, directed by Jeff Feuerzeig, known for "The Devil and Daniel Johnston." The movie is being produced with the band itself — singer Joe Elliott, guitarists Phil Collen and Vivian Campbell, bassist Rick Savage, and drummer Rick Allen — all of whom appear in new interviews.

The film chronicles their rise from humble beginnings in working-class Sheffield, England, to global chart domination in the 1980s and 1990s. Their hits include the Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 smash "Love Bites," plus "Pour Some Sugar on Me" (No. 2), "Armageddon It" (No. 3), and "Hysteria" (No. 10).

Director Feuerzeig's connection goes way back. "In the summer of '81, after reading about Def Leppard in Creem, I saw the not-yet-famous band open for Ozzy Osbourne... at Asbury Park's Convention Hall," he said in a statement. "These young lads from working-class Sheffield were punching far above their weight and playing for keeps. I was smitten, a fan for life."

But the documentary doesn't shy away from the band's darkest chapters. After exploding with albums like "Pyromania" and "Hysteria," they faced two devastating blows: drummer Rick Allen's 1984 car accident, which cost him his arm, and the loss of guitarist Steve Clark in 1991, whose riffs made him a guitar legend. The band rebuilt themselves and became one of rock's most enduring forces.

Feuerzeig calls it a "unique, heartwarming, and often humorous underdog story" — and insists it's "not your typical sex, drugs, and rock 'n' roll tale." The film is produced by VICE Studios, White Horse Pictures, The Searchers Documentary Films, and Sobey Road Entertainment. Def Leppard will play Seminole Hard Rock Live in Hollywood, Florida, on October 15 before touring Mexico, Central, and South America through November. Long live Def Leppard, indeed.
why_it_matters: Music documentaries have become the main way younger listeners meet bands from before they were born, so they quietly decide which acts get remembered and which stories get told; this one also shows how a group rebuilt after a bandmate's disability and another's death — a public template for talking about loss and recovery.

background_read: Def Leppard formed in Sheffield, England, in 1977, part of the same wave of British heavy metal that produced bands like Iron Maiden, and their early albums were made on a tight budget.

Their breakthrough came when producer Robert 'Mutt' Lange (a South African-born hitmaker known for his polished, layered sound) shaped 'Pyromania' and 'Hysteria', albums that turned the group from club act into stadium headliners. 'Hysteria' later became one of the best-selling rock records ever made.

The band's story is also a survival story: drummer Rick Allen lost his left arm in a car crash in 1984 and returned to touring with a specially built electronic drum kit, and guitarist Steve Clark died in 1991, after which Vivian Campbell (previously of the bands Dio and Whitesnake) joined the line-up.

Director Jeff Feuerzeig (best known for 'The Devil and Daniel Johnston', a documentary about an outsider musician) says he first saw the band in the summer of 1981 after reading about them in Creem, a Detroit rock magazine that was hugely influential in the 1970s, when they opened for Ozzy Osbourne (the British singer who had fronted Black Sabbath before going solo).

Films about bands have become a genre in their own right, often released in cinemas for a short run as an event rather than going straight to streaming — and for veteran acts like Def Leppard, who were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2019, they double as a way of reaching listeners born decades after the hits.

perspectives.description: This is the first authorized film, meaning the band gave access and sat for new interviews, which should give fans footage and detail no unofficial film could get. It also gives Sheffield, the band's working-class hometown, a piece of global music history to be proud of and a boost for the city's music tourism.

Authorized documentaries are controlled by their subjects, so critics may argue that messy material gets smoothed over — especially when the director promises something that is 'not your typical sex, drugs, and rock 'n' roll tale'. Releasing it in cinemas also doubles as marketing for the band's Latin American tour, blurring art and commerce.

Veteran rock bands increasingly earn more from documentaries, anniversary tours and residencies than from new albums, because audiences want the familiar hits. A cinema documentary fits that pattern: it packages nostalgia as an event that fans will pay to experience together, and it preserves the band's own version of events for the record.

After the cinematic run the film will almost certainly move to streaming, where it could reach listeners who have never seen the band live. Since Def Leppard entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2019, the documentary may become the standard introduction to them — and a test of whether the rock documentary boom keeps growing or starts to feel repetitive.
